title: NCI Cancer Model Development for the Human Cancer Model Initiative
summary:
The Human Cancer Models Initiative exists to replace ageing immortalised cell lines with models that retain patient genomics and come with their source tumor characterized. Coverage is exceptionally uniform: whole genome on 804 of 805, RNA sequencing on 781, exome on 721, methylation on 703, and both histopathology and radiology on 382.
Its distinctive value is breadth across tumor types, including rare cancers that have no established model system at all. Prior treatment is recorded for 92% of donors, which matters because it determines what the derived model actually represents.
one_liner: 805 next-generation cancer models - organoids and other patient-derived systems - with whole genome sequencing on 804 and the matched patient tumor, spanning many rare cancers.

useful_for.question: How faithfully do patient-derived models retain the genomics of their source tumor?
useful_for.rationale: Models and their source tumors are both characterized, with near-complete whole genome coverage, which makes fidelity measurable rather than assumed. The answer determines how much any model-based result should be trusted.
useful_for.statistical_note: Verify model and source tumor pairing per case; it is not uniform.

evidence.note: Written by a named reviewer after reading the source documentation and the measured field coverage. Not machine-generated.

useful_for.question: Can a usable model system be found for a rare cancer that currently has none?
useful_for.rationale: Coverage spans many tumor types including rare ones. For a researcher working on a cancer with no established cell line, this is often the only route to any model at all, and it is the cohort's most practically valuable use.
useful_for.statistical_note: Per-tumor-type counts are small; this is model discovery, not a powered comparison.

useful_for.question: Does prior treatment of the donor shape the derived model's biology?
useful_for.rationale: Prior treatment is informative for 88.9% of donors and treatment given is recorded for all, so models derived from treated and untreated patients can be compared - a question with direct bearing on how model-based drug screens should be interpreted.

analysis_examples.title: Join the same patients across two NCI repositories
analysis_examples.question: Which cohorts have both imaging and molecular data on the same patients, and how many patients actually carry both?
analysis_examples.problem: Molecular and imaging data for the same cohort live in separate NCI repositories.
analysis_examples.lesson: Join shared patient identifiers and quantify the real multimodal overlap, not the advertised totals.
analysis_examples.figure: Paired horizontal bars per cohort comparing GDC molecular case counts with IDC imaging patient counts, where the shorter bar is the ceiling on a multimodal study of that cohort.
inputs: Open GDC and IDC APIs, no account required
outputs: Patient-level intersection between a GDC project and an IDC collection
Counts of molecular-only, imaging-only and joined patients
A map of every cohort present in both repositories
A chart comparing molecular and imaging patient counts per linkable cohort
steps: Retrieve patient identifiers from the GDC project
Query IDC's public SQL endpoint for the collection's patient identifiers
Intersect on the shared barcode and quantify the overlap
Sweep every GDC project against every IDC collection
findings: All 1,098 TCGA-BRCA patients appear in both the GDC and the IDC, a 100% join with nothing imaging-only.
39 cohorts exist in both repositories, covering 15,761 patients.
HCMI-CMDC holds 805 molecular cases but 382 imaging patients, so its multimodal ceiling is 382, not 805.
